payload.title: What Are the Greek Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
protect_keywords: why do greeks spit at weddings
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a generous budget, often with a Greek-Australian partner or parent, who want to understand each Greek custom in the order it happens, which belong to the Orthodox service and which are family folklore, and what it takes to marry legally in Greece or to hold the customs at home in an Australian Orthodox parish.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed straight after the legal section.
payload.service_link: /magazine (primary, UTM-tagged); /wonderland-concierge (secondary, UTM-tagged, after the legal section)
payload.angle: A Greek wedding has two layers, and page-one listicles blur them: the Orthodox service, whose rites (betrothal and rings, stefana, common cup, Dance of Isaiah) are set out by the Church itself, and the family folklore around it (krevati, names on the shoe, koufeta, plate smashing, the money dance) that is 'often told' and varies by region. We walk 12 customs in the order a couple meets them, from proxenio and engagement to the last kalamatianos, source the service from the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia and goarch.org, label folklore honestly, and finish with what Australians need to marry legally in Greece (civil or religious, municipality, embassy documents, apostille, translation) as at November 2026, plus how Greek-Australian couples hold the same service at home.
must_include: One early framing line: the Orthodox service is set by the Church; the customs around it vary by family and region
Customs in order, grouped Before and at the church / The celebration, each numbered (10 to 12)
The Orthodox service broken into its parts in order (betrothal with rings, candles, crowning with stefana, Gospel and common cup, Dance of Isaiah, removal of crowns) from Archdiocese sources
Koumbaros and koumbara: role in the service and beyond (godparent link only if sourced)

Legal section for Australians marrying in Greece: civil (municipality, dimos) or religious ceremony, documents from the Australian Embassy Athens, apostille and translation, banns only if an official source says so, same-sex civil marriage only from an official Greek source, recognition in Australia, Smartraveller 'Exercise normal safety precautions' (updated 30 September 2026, no higher-level areas), 'as at November 2026', 'check with the municipality and the embassy, including any fees'
Greek-Australian weddings at home: Orthodox parishes in Australia, priest first for dates (fasting periods if sourced)
FAQ of 6 to 8 questions covering the old page's question set (common traditions, spitting, stefana, koufeta, foot stomp, what to wear, what to say, gifts) with no amounts
Links: /destinations/europe/greece hub near the top and in the legal section; re-pointed German and Turkish links with descriptive anchors

tradition_plan.note: Planner (wedding-planner-sme) runs batch A and batch B in parallel, scratch folders 02-research/batch-a and 02-research/batch-b, 15 min HARD by the clock, save after every 3 facts, no extra sourcing rounds. Preferred sources: greekorthodox.org.au (Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia), goarch.org (Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America, sacrament pages), ich.unesco.org, gov.gr and dimos (municipality) pages, greece.embassy.gov.au, smartraveller.gov.au, visitgreece.gr, museums (Benaki, Museum of Greek Folk Art), encyclopaedias (Britannica), peer-reviewed journals. Never competitor wedding sites, vendor blogs, Wikipedia, lifestyle magazines. Unsourced: 'often told', no meanings stated as fact, no [[VERIFY]] marker. Greek terms transliterated as the source gives them. One honest framing line per section.
